extra.message: Flask secret key is hardcoded as the literal string "super secret key". Anyone with source access can forge Flask session cookies and the login session of any user (including admins), bypassing authentication entirely. The key should be loaded from a secret manager or environment variable and be cryptographically random.

extra.message: request.path is interpolated into a template string via f-string and then rendered with render_template_string(). extra.message: GET /accounts/<user_id>/notes fetches all notes (including private ones) for the supplied user_id without verifying that user_id equals current_user.id. Any authenticated user can read another user's private notes by changing the path parameter. The handler must confirm the requested user_id matches the authenticated user (or that the user is otherwise authorized) before returning the notes.

extra.message: update_account copies all submitted form fields (filtered_values) directly onto current_user.__dict__ via update(). The AccountForm includes an 'is_admin' BooleanField, so any logged-in user can submit is_admin=on (even though the checkbox is only rendered for existing admins) to escalate privileges and gain administrator access. Only allowlisted, expected fields should be assigned to the model.

extra.message: The user-controlled 'preferences' cookie is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads() inside the before_request handler (line 112-120), which runs on every request with no authentication required. Because pickle can execute arbitrary code during deserialization, an attacker can craft a malicious cookie to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. Use a safe serialization format such as JSON, and sign/verify cookie contents with itsdangerous.

extra.message: In validate_token(), the registration code supplied by the user (form.registration_code.data) is interpolated directly into a raw SQL query: text(f"SELECT id, code FROM registration_code WHERE code = '{code}'"). An attacker can break out of the quotes (e.g. code=' OR '1'='1) to bypass registration-code validation and register without a valid code. Use bound parameters (text("... WHERE code = :code"), {"code": code}) instead.

extra.message: POST /notes/<note_id>/delete is a state-changing action with no CSRF protection. Flask-WTF's CSRFProtect is never initialized (the app uses plain wtforms.Form, not FlaskForm, and no CSRF tokens are rendered in templates), so an attacker can craft a cross-site auto-submitting form to delete a victim's notes. CSRF protection (CSRFProtect(app) / FlaskForm with csrf_token) should be enabled for all state-changing endpoints.

extra.message: delete_note loads a note by note_id with session.get(Note, note_id) and deletes it without checking that the note belongs to current_user (or that current_user is an admin). Although the home page only renders a delete button for the owner, the route itself does not enforce ownership, so any authenticated user can delete any other user's note (including private notes) by POSTing to /notes/<id>/delete. Verify note.user_id == current_user.id (or is_admin) before deleting.

extra.message: download() calls urllib.request.urlopen(url) with a URL supplied by the user via the /account/image form (ImageForm.url). urlopen supports arbitrary schemes including file:// (allowing read of local files such as /etc/passwd or the app's database.db) and http(s):// against internal hosts, enabling Server-Side Request Forgery. No allowlist of hosts/schemes or network filtering is applied. Validate/allowlist the URL scheme and host, and block private/link-local addresses.

extra.message: Note text is rendered with the | safe filter ({{ note.text | safe }}), disabling Jinja2 auto-escaping. Notes are created through CKEditor (which allows arbitrary HTML) via POST /notes and the home page displays all public notes to every user, so an attacker can store a payload like <script>...</script> in a note that executes in every viewer's browser (stored XSS). Do not mark user content as safe; render it as text or sanitize it server-side.

extra.message: The SQLAlchemy engine is created with echo=True, which logs every SQL statement (including interpolated bound parameter values) to stdout. This exposes sensitive data such as user emails, password-hash lookups, registration codes, and note contents in application logs. Disable echo in production (echo=False) and avoid logging query parameters.
